Disconsolate means deeply, heavily sad — in a way that cannot be comforted or relieved by anything or anyone around you.

The heart of this word is "comfort that doesn't work." When someone is disconsolate, they are in such a state of sorrow that nothing can reach them — not kind words, not hugs, not distractions, not the company of loved ones. The sadness has gone to a place beyond the reach of consolation.

Think of it this way: when a person is sad, we usually try to console them — to comfort them and ease the pain. Sometimes that works. But when someone is disconsolate, it doesn't. They are closed off from all outside help.

Disconsolate describes quite deep sadness. It is far stronger than "upset" or "sad," and sits in similar emotional territory to words like "heartbroken," "devastated," or "inconsolable." Among these, disconsolate carries a particularly still, hollow, and heavy quality. It's not the loud, explosive grief of "devastated" — it's quieter and more sunken than that. Think of a kind of emptied-out unhappiness; the person has not just broken down, they have withdrawn.
It shows in how a person looks, not just how they feel

One distinctive quality of this word is that it describes both a person's internal state and their outward appearance. A disconsolate person looks the part. They might sit silently, staring at nothing. They might refuse food, conversation, or company. They might seem physically weighed down — slumped, hollow-eyed, lost. The word paints a complete picture of a person who has been overtaken by sadness from the inside out, and whose body shows it.

Disconsolate sadness tends to be triggered by real, significant losses or crushing disappointments — the death of a loved one or a pet, the end of an important relationship, a devastating failure after great hope, or a major defeat. It is not the right word for small frustrations or mild unhappiness. Save it for moments of genuine, deep sorrow.
Register: Where will you see or hear this word?

Disconsolate belongs to a slightly formal, literary register. You'll encounter it far more often in novels, journalism, or essays than in casual everyday speech. If you said to a friend, "I'm feeling disconsolate today," it would sound a little elevated. In written English, however, it fits perfectly and carries real weight and precision.

• "After her dog died, she sat disconsolate on the kitchen floor, too hollowed out to even cry."
  • "The team returned from the final disconsolate, unable to speak to one another."
  • "No amount of reassurance could lift his disconsolate mood."
  • "She wandered the empty house in a disconsolate daze, unsure what to do with herself."
  • "The disconsolate widow refused all visitors in the weeks following the funeral."
A picture to hold in your mind

Imagine someone who has just received the worst news of their life. Friends arrive and say kind things. Family brings food. People try jokes, distractions, reassurances. None of it touches them. They sit sunken in their sadness — unreachable, withdrawn, beyond comfort. That person is disconsolate.

If you can hold that image, you have truly understood the word.
